With all the chatter about pronouns I find it odd that no one put forth the theory that Dr. Chuang's gender identity was a contributing factor to Incident 414-A.

The -1s only requirement is that the target show some degree of asociality. It is fairly common for non-conforming personalities (gender based or otherwise) to withdraw from society to a greater or lesser degree. This is sometimes a self-defense mechanism against prejudice and sometimes imposed from outside by the prejudiced avoiding contact. Even if The Foundation as an organization was completely open-minded, this sort of social dynamic could still come up with less modern-thinking coworkers or the civilian public. This could go a long way towards explaining why -1s spoke to Dr. Chuang and not, for example, Dr. Ogawa.

It doesn't strike me as a character choice that actually needs justification. But the fridge-logic hangs together and the theory speaks to the "this doesn't need to be here" category of critique.

Also; Welcome to the NHK, Dr. Chuang!

item.content:encoded:
It is strange and bizarre to me that a good 40% of the discussion on this page is about pronoun usage. I was not bothered or taken out of the article in any way by it.

I'm a super reluctant neutral vote on this. I think that, in terms of theme and idea, this is one of the strongest works on the site. The idea of anomalous social workers targeting asocial NEETs and mindwiping them to make them productive is super interesting. I also really liked the lack of explanation around the super high incidence of suicide among people suffering from 414-2, which at face value means that the stress of not being around people leads to the suicides, but which I personally took to imply that there is some remnant of the person's personality which cannot handle what they have become.

One of the thematic wells that's specific to the SCP Foundation universe that I feel hasn't been tapped too much is that of disability and mental illness; this article draws specific attention to it when the 414-1s are like "hey you and me aren't really that different". So I liked that this article drew a cool parallel between the Foundation drawing a boundary between consensus reality/anomalous and the -1s drawing a boundary between the sick/healthy.

What didn't work for me were the two transcripts. 414-A kind of served to hammer in thematic concepts that I felt were implied more effectively in the description section. I didn't find Chuang's dialogue too believable: their emotion and agitation felt a bit forced. I do like the -1s explaining the utility in suicide, but I feel like there's a more elegant way to integrate that. The conversation between Ogawa and Chuang was likewise hit or miss: I really liked the voice you gave Chuang, but the interview itself fell kind of flat because it was my first exposure to their relationship so I didn't really feel for the loss of it. I have basically zero exposure to Ogawa, so I don't really feel for her character either.

This leaves me, basically, with the most interesting article I've ever novoted. I think, if this were ever to be revised, I'd think it'd be cool if we got a more detailed look at Ogawa and Chuang's relationship. As much as I have a bias against skips that are cursory shells for narratives, I think the actual anomaly and the images it evokes are strong enough to justify some more indulgence on the narrative side of things.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I really liked this. Not much more to say.

Reading up on some comments, I thought I'd weigh in on the gender aspect, which for such a tiny part of this piece sure gets a lot of attention. Why not give it more, I guess?

Warning: Long, rambly. :)

Display Responses
– hide block

Critique #1: For a reader not already familiar with non-binary people, using singular they for a character whose gender is 'known' is confusing.

Response: Sure, but this is true for non-binary people in real life, too. I do agree that if it's a significant part of the story, and aimed at an audience potentially unfamiliar with the concept, then it ought to be explained in the text, at least in brief. I don't think that's the case for this SCP, though.

Otherwise, this is merely part of a larger cultural shift which is ongoing. The only way to further that shift is to just keep usin' non-binary pronouns, rather than try to wait til everyone understands it (a moment which will never come, if they are never used). It's an artistically valid choice, and not sufficiently different from using words or cultural references that people then have to look up.

Critique #2: Making someone non-binary in a story not about being non-binary is a poor artistic choice because being non-binary is so unusual as to draw attention to itself.

Response: Conceptually, "avoid making someone [X unusual trait] in a story not about [X unusual trait]" is an okay rule of thumb.

It has some issues, though. Two occur when you're talking about the real life traits of marginalized people which are (accurately or inaccurately) perceived as unusual:

Firstly, because it leads to bad art: stories dominated by straight white cis dudes, even though they're a tiny percentage of the population, merely because that's what we're used to… and so it's not distracting. (It's not considered distracting when almost no women appear on television or movie screens despite being a majority of the population… yet it's absolutely nonsensical.)

Secondly, because it promotes the negative social trends that marginalizes people with those traits in the first place. Fiction, in aggregate, has a well-known and eminently provable effect on what people perceive about other people in The Real Life. Non-binary people are not even close to as rare as people tend to think, but the way we're talked about, you'd think we barely exist. Well, we don't exist much in fiction!

Yes, people publicly identifying as non-binary is uncommon in general, but certainly much much more common in real life than fiction, and it's super easy to find and meet people like that if you run in the right circles (especially younger, more progressive ones — similar to how older generations don't tend to identify as gay even if they are gay, and positive awareness of gay people has a massive head start on non-binary people).

There's also a third reason not specifically related to marginalized people, which is that it's standard practice, in writing, to give a character specific traits, sometimes unusual traits, to make them seem more like a person than a placeholder. This rule of thumb of 'avoid unusual traits' encourages generic 'placeholder characters' when taken too far.

You still don't want to go over the top with these traits, but being non-binary isn't over the top. You won't find many people with, say, Darkblade style fanfic-y traits, but you can find lots of ordinary boring non-binary people right on this website.

'Avoid writing about non-binary characters unless the story is about them' also gets really weird when you think about it. I mean, I'm non-binary. People largely don't think I exist, but I do. Not everything about my life is about being non-binary. Should all my fiction that contains characters who are non-binary (like me) be about being non-binary? Why do I have to choose between "allowing people like me and my friends to exist in fiction" and "writing stories that aren't centered around non-binary gender"? I think this is a false choice, however well-intended.

In that light, including non-binary characters does not violate economy of characterization.

Put another way: This is how culture changes, and fiction is a major part of culture, one of its biggest engines. These concepts used to be applied to gay people much more when 'your average reader' knew fewer gay people (who were 'out' to them). Now most people know someone who's gay (and this critique still gets used! but never mind that).

Critique #3: While non-binary gender has existed since gender existed (easy enough to google), it has been nearly unknown in modern Western culture until very recently. It's unrealistic that a massive, bureaucratic, slow-to-change, conservative organization like the Foundation would acknowledge or allow non-binary pronouns in official documentation.

This is a better argument. The Foundation is massive, bureaucratic, slow-to-change, and conservative by its nature ('conservative' is more controversial but IMO it's kind of baked into an organization literally preserving how things are right now).

But this argument still misses other core aspects of the Foundation. To wit:

  • The Foundation also has to deal with incredibly unusual things, all the time, constantly, forever. And … unusual minds tend to study unusual things. And be more open to things people consider unusual. Yes, sometimes people who deal with the unusual instead double down on normativity, but sometimes they don't. Making this an issue of headcanon. (In which case, why do you choose to make the creative choice of picking one or the other?)
    • Just look how many people in the Foundation community are willing to identify themselves as non-binary. Not more than exist in the general population, but more than are usually willing to publicly admit it, or have those pronouns acknowledged. Same for queer people. It's almost become an in-joke in real life how real-life Foundation writers and staff members tend to be disproportionately queer or trans compared to the general writing population. Why not apply this to in-universe Foundation staff members? Why should they be more 'reflective of the average' than the people actually writing the fiction?
  • It's a scientific organization run largely by scientists. Scientists have a serious traditional streak, but they also have a serious openness to change, one which cannot be equaled even in the arts. They always have to be open to their hypotheses being falsified, at least in theory.
    • Look at how US scientists adopted metric — when it's unimaginable that the non-scientist US population will do so anytime soon. Yes, this isn't quite the same thing because it has direct immediate effects on procedures, but notice also how scientists near-universally acknowledged that being gay was perfectly okay (and natural) far, far in advance of wider culture doing so (arguably wider culture has only done this to some extent in the past few years, looking at statistics on acceptance of gay marriage, but scientists caught up with that decades ago). There also have been scientists acknowledging non-binary gender already; it hasn't ballooned as big as sexuality did yet, but judging from trends and early signs, it's only a matter of time.
  • A distinct minority of headcanons take the Foundation as more military than scientific. In this case, the argument is both stronger, and weaker. Stronger because the US military has extremely conservative perspectives overall on gender (and everything, really), and are demonstrably terribly slow to change. Weaker because, as we see with the current integration of women into the military, all you need to change everything below you is the say-so of the right figures with Absolute Power. In which case, it becomes more a matter of headcanon — "Maybe there's a trans-friendly O5 who pretty much declared This Is What We Do Now, got enough of the other O5s on board, and the rest of the Foundation had to go along with it." (Note: At least one and maybe two of the O5s are trans in the Resurrection canon, as a not-so-random example.)

Personally, I tend to present the in-universe Foundation as in some ways reflective of the real-life Foundation community. There are people who are confused by non-binary/trans gender (and misgender others by accident); there are people who actively dislike non-binary/trans people being part of (or acknowledged as part of) the organization, even rhetorically comparing them to anomalies or Serpent's Hand types; there are people who are non-binary/trans and are quiet about it in one way or another; there are people who are non-binary/trans and are open about it in one way or another; there are people who actively campaign for official documentation and standards & practices to use proper pronouns when appropriate.

I assume any assortment of members of each group are powerful and well-placed. I pick which groups have 'won out' within the Foundation (or specific area of the Foundation) based on what story and situation I'm writing.

I hope you enjoyed this wall of text!

item.content:encoded:
Making someone nonbinary when it isn't important to the story seems like an odd characterization choice as nonbinary individuals are statistically much rarer than individuals with binary identity. I believe in a economy of characterization where you shouldn't make a character any more unusual than you need to, especially if the only thing you are going to do with the characterization is pronoun choice.

Both using plural pronouns for individuals and acknowledging nonbinary gender identity at all are relatively new concepts and large organizations like the Foundation are notoriously slow at adopting things like that, so it seems unlikely to me that the internal style that the Foundation requires reports in would include it. Equivalent styles in US Government reports, as an example, do not presently do so, by my understanding.

I suspect that my opinion is offensive to you, and I want to stress that seeing a Dr. Eliza Chuang referred to with a plural pronoun was odd to me in this context, for the reasons given above. I was initially confused as to whom it was referring. I am not saying that it is by any means incorrect, though.
